title: WHY DOES PAUL SAY A WIFE HAS AUTHORITY OVER HER HUSBAND’S BODY TOO?
paragraphs: WHY DOES PAUL SAY A WIFE HAS AUTHORITY OVER HER HUSBAND’S BODY TOO?
The verse that sounds shocking until you notice what Paul did to male privilege—and how the Gospel turns marriage from possession into mutual self-giving love.
There is a sentence in the Bible that many husbands have heard quoted.
Far fewer have heard the other half.
And leaving out that other half can turn something beautiful into something dangerous.
Paul writes:
Some people stop there.
Conveniently.
But Paul does not.
He immediately turns the sentence around:
“Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.”
—1 Corinthians 7:4
Read that again.
The husband does not have authority over his own body.
The wife does.
For readers accustomed to hearing Christianity portrayed as though biblical marriage simply gives a husband power while requiring a wife to surrender hers, Paul’s actual words can be startling.
But the Greek is even more revealing.
Paul writes:
ἡ γυνὴ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλὰ ὁ ἀνήρ· ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τοῦ ἰδίου σώματος οὐκ ἐξουσιάζει ἀλλὰ ἡ γυνή.
A careful translation is:
“The wife does not exercise authority over her own body, but the husband does; and likewise also the husband does not exercise authority over his own body, but the wife does.”
That word translated “has authority” or “exercises authority” comes from ἐξουσιάζω (exousiazō), a verb connected with authority or having rights over something.
But perhaps the most important word for understanding Paul’s point is much smaller:
ὁμοίως.
Homoiōs.
“Likewise.”
“In the same way.”
Paul refuses to make the principle travel in only one direction.
Whatever responsibility he places upon the wife, he places reciprocally upon the husband.
And that matters enormously.
Because 1 Corinthians 7 is not a biblical permission slip for a husband to demand sexual access to his wife.
It is not divine authorization for coercion.
It is not Scripture telling a frightened spouse that “no” is rebellion against God.
It is certainly not permission for abuse.
Paul is describing the astonishing mutuality of the marriage covenant.
And to understand why, we need to hear what was happening before verse 4.

The Corinthian Christians had questions about sex, marriage, celibacy, and holiness. Some apparently regarded sexual abstinence—even within marriage—as spiritually desirable. Paul responds not by portraying marital intimacy as dirty, but by affirming the reciprocal responsibilities of husband and wife.
Listen to the symmetry:
“The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband.”
—1 Corinthians 7:3
Again:
Likewise.
Then comes verse 4. Her body belongs covenantally to him—and his body belongs covenantally to her.
Then Paul continues:
“Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; but then come together again…”
—1 Corinthians 7:5
And there is the detail that must never disappear from this conversation:
“by agreement.”
The Greek word is συμφώνου—related to symphōnos, meaning agreement or mutual consent.
It is the idea behind our word “symphony.”
Not one instrument crushing another.
Agreement.
Harmony.
Together.
Paul could hardly have constructed the paragraph more reciprocally.
The husband gives.
The wife gives.
The wife does not treat her body as though marriage has no claim upon her.
The husband does not treat his body as though marriage has no claim upon him.
Neither should deprive the other selfishly.
And periods of abstinence are approached by agreement.
Paul is not handing one spouse a weapon.
He is taking selfishness away from both.
That distinction changes everything.
Because sinful humanity hears “authority” and immediately asks:
“What can I demand?”
Jesus teaches us to ask:
“What can I give?”
That is the heartbeat of Christian marriage.
Not possession.
Self-giving.
Not domination.
Sacrificial love.
Not “Your body exists for my gratification.”
But:
“I am no longer living as though my desires are the only desires that matter.”
And husbands especially cannot separate 1 Corinthians 7 from the wider New Testament picture of Christlike love.
Paul tells husbands:
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
—Ephesians 5:25
Notice the direction of Christ’s love.
He gave Himself.
The model placed before the Christian husband is not a king sitting comfortably on a throne demanding service.
It is Jesus Christ laying Himself down.
A cross.
Sacrifice.
Tenderness.
Holiness.
Love willing to bleed for the good of another.
So imagine the tragedy when someone takes 1 Corinthians 7:4—a verse built around mutual self-giving—and uses it to justify selfish taking.
The text has been turned upside down.
A husband cannot faithfully say, “Your body belongs to me,” while conveniently forgetting that Paul says his body belongs to her too.
And neither spouse should turn Paul’s language into ammunition.
Marriage is not two people standing across the bedroom shouting biblical claims of ownership at one another.
It is two people learning, imperfectly, to say:
“I belong to Christ, and because I have covenanted myself to you, I will not live as though only my comfort, appetite, schedule, fear, exhaustion, pleasure, or preference matters.”
That does not eliminate bodily dignity.
It deepens covenant responsibility.
There may be illness.
Pain.
Trauma.
Pregnancy.
Postpartum recovery.
Medication.
Disability.
Hormonal changes.
Emotional wounds.
Exhaustion.
A spouse may need patience, safety, conversation, medical care, counseling, repentance, restoration, or simply tenderness.
Biblical love does not bulldoze those realities with a verse.
Love listens.
Love does not dishonor.
Love “does not insist on its own way” (1 Corinthians 13:5).
That sentence alone should make us tremble before using Scripture selfishly.
Because the same apostle who writes that spouses have marital claims upon one another’s bodies also writes that love does not insist upon its own way.
There is no contradiction.
There is covenant.
There is the difference between demanding and giving.
Between entitlement and devotion.
Between using another person and becoming one flesh with another person.
And perhaps this passage is exposing something much deeper than what happens in a bedroom.
Maybe the uncomfortable question is not:
“Does my spouse owe me?”
Maybe it is:
“How much of myself am I still refusing to surrender?”
Because selfishness rarely stays in one room.
It appears when you stop listening.
When affection becomes conditional.
When resentment becomes punishment.
When silence becomes a weapon.
When pornography secretly rewrites your expectations.
When flirtation outside the marriage begins feeding an appetite you promised to guard.
When a husband expects tenderness he refuses to give.
When a wife uses distance to punish rather than communicate.
When either spouse begins keeping an invisible ledger:
I did this.
So you owe me that.
Then marriage slowly stops looking like covenant and starts looking like commerce.
And Jesus did not save us so that we could become expert accountants of what other people owe us.
The Gospel destroys the illusion that love is merely a transaction.
At the cross, Christ does not merely tell sinners to love.
He shows us what holy love costs.
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
—Romans 5:8
There is the center.
Jesus.
Not sex.
Not marital power.
Not winning an argument.
Jesus.
Because even the healthiest Christian marriage is not the Gospel.
Marriage points beyond itself to something greater.
Christ and His people.
A Savior who pursues sinners not to exploit them but to redeem them.
A Bridegroom who gives Himself for His bride.
A Lord whose authority is perfectly holy and whose sacrifice reaches all the way to Calvary.
And suddenly Paul's words become more uncomfortable in the right way.
The question is no longer:
“How much authority do I have over my spouse?”
The question becomes:
“Has Jesus transformed the way I use whatever power, strength, influence, sexuality, affection, and freedom I possess?”
That question can expose a marriage.
It can expose a husband who knows Bible verses but has forgotten tenderness.
It can expose a wife carrying years of resentment she has never brought honestly into the light.
It can expose hidden pornography.
Secret messages.
Emotional affairs.
Manipulation.
Bitterness.
Coldness.
Shame.
Fear.
Past wounds.
It can expose two people sleeping inches apart while their souls feel miles away.
Maybe nobody knows.
Sunday comes.
You dress nicely.
You smile.
You sit beside each other.
Someone asks how the family is doing.
“Good.”
But God knows what “good” is hiding.
He sees the silence on the drive home.
He sees the screen you quickly close.
He sees the nights one of you quietly cries.
He sees the rejection that became bitterness and the bitterness that became distance.
He sees the apologies that never came.
He sees the words you wish you could take back.
He sees the loneliness nobody at church notices.
And He does not expose darkness because He delights in humiliating you.
He calls darkness into the light because Jesus came to save sinners.
That is where scandal can become grace.
Not when we pretend the scandal never happened.
When we bring it to Christ.
Christian repentance is not saying, “Nobody is perfect.”
It is saying:
“Lord, this is sin. I have no excuse. Forgive me. Change me.”
Grace is not God pretending our sin does not matter.
Grace cost the blood of Jesus Christ.
At Calvary, Christ bore sin so sinners could be forgiven, reconciled to God, and transformed.
That means the controlling husband can repent.
The bitter wife can repent.
The pornography-addicted spouse can repent.
The emotionally absent spouse can repent.
The person who weaponized Scripture can repent.
The person who withheld affection to punish can repent.
The person carrying shame from what was done to them can discover that another person's sin does not place them beyond Christ's compassion.

And where there has been abuse or coercion, repentance must never be reduced to religious language that pressures the harmed spouse into immediate trust or unsafe reconciliation. Serious wrongdoing requires truth, accountability, protection, and appropriate pastoral, professional, and when necessary legal help. Forgiveness does not require pretending danger is safe.
Jesus does not need us to hide evil in order to protect Christianity.
He is the Light.
Bring it into the light.
That may be the word someone reading this has avoided for years.
Light.
No more hiding.
No more performing.
No more carefully edited Christianity.
Maybe your marriage needs a conversation tonight.
Maybe you need to say:
“I have been selfish.”
“I have not listened to you.”
“I used Scripture to win instead of allowing Scripture to change me.”
“I have made you feel unwanted.”
“I have made you feel unsafe.”
“I have been hiding something.”
“I need help.”
“I was wrong.”
“Will you forgive me?”
Those sentences can feel terrifying.
But sometimes resurrection begins where pretending finally dies.
Not because strangers need the details of your private life.
They do not.
But sometimes three words become a line in the sand between the person who keeps pretending and the person who finally admits:
Jesus, I need You to change me.
Let believers pray without demanding your private story.
Someone else may desperately need to know that restoration is possible.
Not as a performance.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not our works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But if Christ has given you truth that may rescue another person from distortion, shame, selfishness, or despair, sharing that truth can become an act of love.
“Is this really what the Bible teaches?”
Someone may have had Scripture weaponized against them.
Someone may be destroying a marriage through selfishness while calling it biblical authority.
Someone may believe what they have done is too ugly for Jesus to forgive.
Let this reach them.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelievers to follow too.
Supporting Gospel Warrior should never be confused with earning God's favor. You cannot purchase grace, and God is not glorified by manipulation.
But whatever you do after reading this, do not miss Paul’s point.
He was never teaching husbands how to take more.
He was teaching husbands and wives that covenant love means selfishness no longer gets the final word.
Your spouse is not an object.
Not an entitlement.
Not a reward.
Not a servant assigned to satisfy your desires.
They are a person made in the image of God.
And Christian marriage calls two redeemed sinners to learn something the flesh desperately resists:
mutual self-giving love.
You will fail at it sometimes.
So will your spouse.
There will be misunderstandings.
There may be tears.
There may be seasons when intimacy feels effortless and seasons when loving one another requires extraordinary patience.
But Christ remains.
And where sin has written chapters of selfishness, shame, betrayal, resentment, or broken trust, Jesus is still able to write repentance.
Forgiveness.
Truth.
Holiness.
Healing.
Grace.
Maybe that is why this difficult verse is more beautiful than we realized.
Paul did not merely tell a wife:
“You are not your own.”
He looked at the husband and said:
Neither are you.
Likewise.
ὁμοίως.
One small Greek word.
One devastating blow to selfish entitlement.
One reminder that beneath the cross, Christian marriage cannot faithfully become a kingdom where one sinner exists for the comfort of another.
Both belong first to Christ.
Both are called to love.
Both are called away from selfishness.
Both need grace.
And both must remember that the Savior at the center of their covenant did not conquer His bride by exploiting her.
He loved her.
He gave Himself for her.
He died.
And He rose again.
So before you ask what your spouse owes you, stand beneath the cross long enough to remember what Jesus gave for you.
Because sometimes the marriage Jesus begins restoring is the one where two people finally stop asking, “What am I owed?” and kneel before Christ asking, “Lord, what in me still needs to die?”
